papers.title: Therapeutic Hybrid Intelligence with Neural and Knowledge-based Expert Reasoning for SRS (THINKERS): an AI model for melanoma brain metastases.
papers.abstract: Dose selection for melanoma brain metastases treated with stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) remains largely based on generalized practice patterns rather than tumor-specific modeling of local failure dynamics. We developed a Therapeutic Hybrid Intelligence with Neural and Knowledge-based Expert Reasoning for SRS (THINKERS) in Melanoma Brain Metastases, an artificial intelligence framework for prognostic prediction. We performed a retrospective single-center study of melanoma brain metastases treated with SRS at UPMC. Only variables available at or before treatment were included. The final model used a mixture-of-experts deep neural network with discrete-time survival modeling. Margin dose was incorporated as an explicit input variable, allowing repeated evaluation across candidate dose levels for tumor-specific dose evaluation. Internal validation consisted of grouped 5-fold cross-validation and a grouped holdout test split by patient. The final analytic cohort included 141 patients with 884 treated melanoma brain metastases. Median age at treatment was 65 years (IQR, 55-74), median pre-treatment KPS was 70 (IQR, 60-70), and median tumor volume was 0.133 cm3 (IQR, 0.047-0.624). In the grouped holdout test set, the model achieved an AUC of 0.807 (patient-cluster bootstrap 95% CI, 0.714-0.892 and an MAE of 1.47 months (95% CI, 1.18-1.75). Probabilistic performance was favorable, with a Brier score of 0.077, calibration intercept of 0.129, and calibration slope of 0.833, indicating good discrimination, low overall prediction error, and acceptable calibration. THINKERS-Melanoma provides an internally validated framework for patient-specific SRS dose comparison in melanoma brain metastases and supports the feasibility of AI-guided radiosurgical evaluation.

papers.title: Development of a novel RNA modification-based risk model to predict prognosis and immunotherapy response in melanoma using machine learning.
papers.abstract: Melanoma is a highly malignant cancer that poses a significant global health burden, yet there is limited ability to predict prognosis or immunotherapy efficacy for melanomas. Emerging evidence highlights the role of RNA modification regulators (m6A, m1A, m5C, and m7G) in modulating oncogenesis and immune responses. We comprehensively profiled 84 regulators of RNA modification (m6A/m1A/m5C/m7G) across multiple melanoma cohorts. Unsupervised clustering was performed to identify RNA modification-based subtypes, followed by WGCNA to reveal key modules. We developed the RMODscore prognostic model using LASSO and multivariate Cox regression and validated the model in several independent melanoma immunotherapy cohorts. Finally, we explored the association of RMODscore with immune signatures and drug sensitivity. We found significant differences in survival among three different RNA modification subtypes and identified the ME13 module as significantly associated with these subtypes using the WGCNA method. Our newly constructed 10-gene RMODscore model showed strong predictive performance in the TCGA cohort and four independent immunotherapy datasets. A high RMODscore was associated with poor survival, immune-cold phenotypes, and resistance to checkpoint blockade. Functional analysis revealed that tumors with high RMODscore values exhibited upregulation of proliferation-related pathways, whereas tumors with low RMODscore values exhibited greater immune activation. In addition, the RMODscore predicted sensitivity to ERK and JNK inhibitors, suggesting potential drug repurposing strategies. This study presents a novel RNA modification-based prognostic risk score as a robust prognostic tool for melanoma which may provide potential prognostic stratification value. These findings highlight the potential of RNA modification signatures for prognostic stratification and may provide preliminary insights for future therapeutic strategy exploration in patients with melanoma.
papers.journal: Journal of cancer research and clinical oncology

papers.title: A rare presentation of metastatic thymic carcinoma mimicking pheochromocytoma and Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome: a case report.
papers.abstract: Metastatic thymic carcinoma is a rare and aggressive malignancy that may present with atypical clinical and biochemical features, posing significant diagnostic challenges. We report the first documented case of metastatic thymic carcinoma mimicking both pheochromocytoma and Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome. A 54-year-old man presented with neck pain, microscopic hematuria, bilateral adrenal masses, fluctuating hypertension, and borderline elevated plasma normetanephrine, raising suspicion for pheochromocytoma. Concurrent retinal abnormalities and cerebellar lesions suggested VHL syndrome. However, serial biochemical reassessment demonstrated normalization of catecholamine metabolites, while ophthalmologic evaluation reclassified the retinal findings as hypertensive retinopathy rather than retinal hemangioblastoma. Brain imaging showed features atypical for VHL-associated hemangioblastomas. ^68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT demonstrated no significant tracer uptake in the adrenal or cerebellar lesions but revealed increased somatostatin receptor expression in an anterior mediastinal mass with tracer-avid lymph node and skeletal metastases. Histopathological examination of an adrenal mass confirmed metastatic basaloid squamous thymic carcinoma (CK5/6-positive, p63-positive, synaptophysin-negative, chromogranin-negative), excluding a neuroendocrine origin. This case highlights the remarkable ability of metastatic thymic carcinoma to mimic endocrine and hereditary syndromes, resulting in potential diagnostic pitfalls. A systematic diagnostic approach integrating serial biochemical testing, advanced functional imaging, comprehensive clinical reassessment, and histopathological confirmation is essential to establish the correct diagnosis. Metastatic thymic carcinoma should be considered in the differential diagnosis of adrenal masses with syndromic features, even when the initial presentation strongly suggests pheochromocytoma or VHL syndrome.

papers.title: Incretin-Based Therapies in Prostate Cancer: From Metabolic Protection to Potential Antitumour Activity - A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: This narrative review evaluates the clinical rationale for integrating incretin-based therapies as therapeutic adjuncts for men with advanced prostate cancer undergoing androgen axis suppression. Androgen deprivation therapy combined with potent androgen receptor pathway inhibitors significantly prolongs survival but induces severe, progressive metabolic toxicities, including sarcopenic obesity, profound insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and heightened cardiovascular mortality. To address this unmet need, this study reviews published preclinical mechanisms, epidemiological data, and emerging clinical datasets examining glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists. The compiled evidence indicates that these agents provide robust metabolic protection by counteracting treatment-induced metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular risk. Furthermore, incretins may exert indirect antitumor effects by attenuating systemic hyperinsulinemia and visceral adiposity-driven chronic inflammation. Direct antitumor activity is also supported by preclinical evidence demonstrating that receptor engagement on malignant cells downregulates oncogenic signaling pathways, which correlates with recent retrospective clinical database trends showing a numerical reduction in metastatic stage migration among men with localized disease. However, dual receptor agonism introduces mechanistic uncertainty due to potential proliferative signaling cascades in neuroendocrine tumor phenotypes. In conclusion, incretin-based therapies offer a highly rational dual-action strategy for metabolic rescue and potential tumor suppression in advanced prostate cancer. Although several early-phase prospective clinical trials are currently underway to evaluate safety and metabolic efficacy, routine clinical implementation cannot be recommended until rigorously designed randomized controlled trials definitively establish long-term safety, optimal patient selection, and durable oncological outcomes.

papers.title: Submucosal Tunnel Endoscopic Resection of a Gastric Schwannoma Mimicking a Submucosal Tumor.
papers.abstract: Gastric schwannomas are rare benign mesenchymal tumors originating from Schwann cells of the myenteric plexus, accounting for less than 0.2% of all gastric neoplasms. They are often asymptomatic but may present with abdominal pain, bleeding, or obstructive symptoms when large. Endoscopic ultrasound is crucial for preoperative evaluation, while definitive diagnosis relies on histopathology and immunohistochemistry, typically showing strong S-100 protein positivity and negativity for CD117, DOG-1, and smooth muscle actin. Traditional management for symptomatic or large lesions has been surgical resection. However, submucosal tunnel endoscopic resection has emerged as a promising minimally invasive alternative. A case of a 73-year-old female with recurrent abdominal distension is presented, in whom esophagogastroduodenoscopy identified an 8.2 mm submucosal tumor in the gastric body, and endoscopic ultrasound confirmed origin from the muscularis propria. The patient underwent submucosal tunnel endoscopic resection, which involved creating a submucosal tunnel to access and resect the tumor while preserving the overlying mucosa. The procedure was completed successfully without perforation or significant bleeding. Histopathological and immunohistochemical examination confirmed a benign schwannoma with S-100 positive and CD117 and DOG-1 negative staining. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 6 without complications. At 14-month follow-up, no recurrence was observed. This case demonstrates the feasibility and safety of STER in a carefully selected patient with a gastric schwannoma, with minimal mucosal injury and no postoperative complications.

papers.title: The ENETS Framework for Somatostatin Receptor PET Response Assessment in Neuroendocrine Tumors.
Renal autotransplantation for pheochromocytoma involving the renal hilar vessels with kidney preservation: a case report and literature review.
papers.abstract: Pheochromocytomas are neuroendocrine tumors of the adrenal medulla that frequently secrete excessive catecholamines. When such tumors involve the renal hilar vessels, ipsilateral nephrectomy has traditionally been preferred, as in situ dissection risks major vascular injury and massive catecholamine release. This study presents a 37-year-old man with a left adrenal pheochromocytoma presenting with a hypertensive crisis (blood pressure 260/110 mmHg). Intraoperatively, the tumor was found to encase the left renal artery and adhere densely to the left renal vein, so the kidney could not be preserved in situ. The left kidney was removed for ex vivo cold perfusion and bench preparation, the tumor was resected in situ, and the kidney was autotransplanted into the left iliac fossa. Histopathology confirmed a pheochromocytoma with malignant potential. At the 2-year follow-up, blood pressure and renal function remained normal without antihypertensive medication, with no evidence of recurrence. Renal autotransplantation combined with ex vivo bench surgery is a feasible kidney-preserving strategy for pheochromocytomas involving the renal hilar vessels.

papers.title: When genetics disrupt the gut: Dysmotility and ganglioneuromatosis in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B syndrome.
papers.abstract: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2B (MEN2B) is a rare hereditary cancer syndrome characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma, mucosal neuromas, and pheochromocytoma. Gastrointestinal involvement is common and often manifests as diffuse intestinal ganglioneuromatosis (IGN), which can impair motility and lead to severe constipation, pseudo-obstruction, or megacolon. We report a male infant with known MEN2B who developed progressive abdominal distension and obstructive symptoms refractory to medical management. Initial rectal suction biopsies were unrevealing. Due to persistent symptoms, a diverting ileostomy was created for decompression, during which full-thickness biopsies were obtained, ultimately establishing the definitive diagnosis of colonic ganglioneuromatosis. This case highlights the limitations of mucosal biopsies in detecting deeper neural pathology and underscores the importance of maintaining clinical suspicion for IGN in patients with MEN2B and persistent gastrointestinal symptoms despite a normal initial evaluation.

papers.title: Closing the adaptive window: immune-metabolic strategies to constrain melanoma therapy resistance.
papers.abstract: Melanoma cells respond to therapy not only through selection of pre-existing resistant clones, but also by rapidly engaging reversible adaptive programs that preserve viability under treatment. These programs connect signaling rewiring, metabolic plasticity, inflammatory responses, cell-state transitions and remodeling of the tumor microenvironment. We propose that this early adaptive phase creates a temporal and biological window in which melanoma cells acquire sufficient fitness to persist and subsequently evolve more stable epigenetic and genetic resistance. We first examine the rapid signaling responses elicited by MAPK pathway inhibition and the adaptive programs induced by immune-mediated pressure, emphasizing multifunctional hubs that integrate growth, stress, metabolic and inflammatory cues. We then discuss the metabolic flexibility of melanoma cells, including mitochondrial respiration, glutamine and lipid utilization, redox control and NAD/NAMPT-dependent immunometabolic regulation. Finally, we consider therapeutic vaccination and microbiome modulation as complementary strategies that may broaden anti-tumor immunity and reshape treatment responsiveness. Thus, this review focuses primarily on convergent adaptive processes that define this biological window and explores whether their experimental characterization may reveal opportunities to therapeutically constrain adaptive capacity through rationally timed combinations or sequential interventions. Closing the adaptive window may reduce the evolutionary opportunities available to melanoma cells before heterogeneous, fixed resistance mechanisms become established.

papers.title: A Diagnostic Conundrum: A Hemorrhagic Adrenal Mass With Discordant Radiological, Biochemical, and Pathologic Features.
papers.abstract: Adrenal incidentalomas vary in their identity, making accurate diagnosis essential for management. Interpretation of these lesions using radiology, biochemistry, or pathology can be confounded by hemorrhagic changes, medication effects, and limitations of imaging. To prevent misclassification, an integrated assessment is crucial. We present a case of a 71-year-old male with an incidentally discovered left adrenal mass that exhibited computed tomography and MRI imaging findings concerning for pheochromocytoma or adrenal malignancy. Biochemical analysis ruled out pheochromocytoma and was suggestive of possible glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid co-secretion, although clinical urgency of surgical resection precluded completion of confirmatory endocrinologic testing. The lesion was initially diagnosed as a benign endothelial adrenal cyst on pathologic review. Because of the discordance among the radiological, biochemical, and initial pathologic findings, an integrated histologic re-evaluation was requested. The mass was ultimately reclassified as an adrenocortical adenoma with extensive hemorrhagic and cystic changes. This case highlights the importance of multidisciplinary integration when evaluating adrenal lesions with confounding features and underscores how suggestive (though incomplete) biochemical evidence can appropriately drive pathological re-evaluation.

papers.title: Bilateral Adrenal Masses, Extreme Catecholamine Excess, and Hypercalcitoninemia With Metastatic Neuroendocrine Neoplasia: A Diagnostic Dilemma.
papers.abstract: A 40-year-old man presented with back pain, urinary retention, mild unilateral weakness, weight loss, hypercalcemia, and newly recognized hypertension. During the early admission, blood pressure became markedly labile, reaching 225/106 mmHg. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated approximately 10-cm bilateral heterogeneous adrenal masses and diffuse lytic skeletal metastases. Biochemical testing showed profound catecholamine excess, including urine metanephrine/creatinine 42,040 µg/g creatinine (reference range: 29-158 µg/g), normetanephrine/creatinine 6,079 µg/g creatinine (reference range: 53-659 µg/g), and vanillylmandelic acid/creatinine 212 mg/g creatinine (reference range: 1.1-4.1 mg/g). Serum calcitonin was 4,680 pg/mL (reference ≤8.4), with carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) 239 ng/mL (reference <3.8 ng/mL for a non-smoker). Expert review of a bone biopsy showed a metastatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor, WHO grade 3 (2017), with Ki-67 approximately 40%. The tumor expressed chromogranin, synaptophysin, pancytokeratin, thyroid transcription factor 1 (TTF-1), CEA, paired box 8 (PAX8), and cytokeratin (CK) 7 but was negative for calcitonin, thyroglobulin, CK20, GATA3, and S100. Small polypoid lesions at the tip of the tongue, considered possible mucosal neuromas, together with thyroid calcifications raised concern for multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B; however, thyroid fine-needle aspiration, RET testing, and functional imaging were not completed before rapid clinical deterioration. The patient received alpha-blockade, palliative spinal radiotherapy, and carboplatin/etoposide; his course was complicated by profound pancytopenia, extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli bacteremia, respiratory and renal failure, gastrointestinal bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage, and death. The case illustrates clinicopathologic discordance: the biochemical phenotype strongly favored pheochromocytoma, whereas metastatic-site histology did not establish the primary site.

papers.title: Clinical features and outcomes of MEN2A with RET codon 634 pathogenic variants.
papers.abstract: Germline RET codon 634 pathogenic variants (PVs) are at high-risk for early-onset medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), but prior reports suggest that RET p.C634R PV may confer a more aggressive phenotype. We compared MEN2A phenotype and MTC outcomes with germline RET p.C634R vs other RET p.C634X PVs. We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study of patients harboring a germline RET p.C634 PV, enrolled in the MTC Collaborative Registry (MTCCoRe) and seen at least once between May 2012 and May 2024. One hundred and thirty-five patients included: p.C634R (n = 60) and other p.C634X variants (n = 75). The p.C634R PV was associated with higher penetrance of pheochromocytoma (PHEO) (67% vs 37%, P < .001) and primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) (30% vs 15%, P = .036). Prevalence of MTC (87% vs 80%, P = .362), cutaneous lichen amyloidosis (17% vs 9% P = .296), and median age at initial thyroidectomy (18 vs 20 years, P = .479) did not differ significantly between groups. Medullary thyroid carcinoma characteristics, including stage, multifocality, extrathyroidal extension, vascular invasion, lymph node metastases, and distant metastases, were comparable. There were no significant differences in disease-free survival, overall survival, or distant metastasis-free survival for MTC. Disease status at last follow-up also was similar between p.C634R and other p.C634X PVs: no evidence of disease in 43% vs 62% (P = .059), biochemical evidence of disease in 25% vs 17% (P = .226), and structural evidence of disease in 27% vs 20% (P = .298). In this large single-center cohort, germline RET p.C634R was associated with a higher penetrance of PHEO and PHPT but did not increase MTC aggressiveness or worsen clinical outcomes compared with other RET p.C634 PVs.

papers.title: Case Report: Neurosurgery, octreotide, cabergoline, radiotherapy, pasireotide and pegvisomant - a multimodal strategy for adolescent acrogigantism.
papers.abstract: Growth hormone (GH)-secreting pituitary neuroendocrine tumors (PitNETs) are rare in the pediatric population. They often present as large, invasive tumors and are frequently associated with an underlying genetic predisposition, making their management particularly challenging. Optimal treatment requires an individualized multidisciplinary approach, which often involves a combination of surgery and adjuvant medical therapy or radiotherapy when necessary. We present a challenging case of an adolescent female with acrogigantism. The patient was diagnosed at the age of 13 years and 10 months during the evaluation of chronic headaches. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed an invasive PitNET measuring 38 × 23 × 32 mm, while biochemical assessment confirmed marked GH hypersecretion. The disease followed an aggressive course, and biochemical control could not be achieved despite optimal multimodal therapy. Sequential treatment included neurosurgical resection, octreotide LAR, cabergoline, pasireotide LAR, proton beam radiotherapy, and pegvisomant. Combination therapy with pegvisomant and octreotide LAR ultimately normalized insulin-like growth factor 1 concentrations while maintaining long-term radiological tumor stability. This case underscores the complexity of managing aggressive GH-secreting PitNETs in adolescents and emphasizes the need for individualized, multidisciplinary care and long-term follow-up. Combined medical therapy with pegvisomant and octreotide LAR may provide effective biochemical control when surgery, radiotherapy, and standard medical treatment are insufficient.

papers.title: Common Symptom with Rare Entity.
papers.abstract: Paragangliomas are extremely rare neuroendocrine neoplasms with an incidence of 2-8 per million. They mostly present as headache, hypertension, palpitations and diaphoresis. CT scan and MRI abdomen helps in the diagnosis and Positron Emission Tomography (PET) helps to rule out malignancy. Paragangliomas are diagnosed on clinical history, biochemical parameters and radiological imaging but rarely requires histopathology. Surgery is the gold standard treatment which should be performed as early as possible. Here we are reporting the case of young female patient at the age of 18 years presenting with atypical symptoms. Paragangliomas is rare with complex entity which requires a wide approach.

papers.title: Genetic Correlates of Malignant Behavior in Aggressive Pituitary Tumors.
papers.abstract: Aggressive pituitary neuroendocrine tumors (PitNETs) that progress despite surgery, radiotherapy (RT), and medical therapy are heterogenous; only a subset exhibits overtly malignant behavior. We examined genetic determinants of metastatic behavior and poor prognosis. Retrospective genomic cohort study of 39 patients (62 tumor samples) with aggressive PitNETs. Next-generation sequencing was performed using the MSK-IMPACT platform on a sequencing protocol. Genetic alterations were correlated with metastatic status, and progression-free and overall survival (PFS and OS) from first progression following RT. Cell-cycle alterations were found in 23.1% of patients and were more frequently identified in metastatic compared to non-metastatic tumors (42.1% vs 5.0%; OR=12.9; p=0.008). TP53, ATRX, DAXX, and/or SF3B1 alterations were associated with adverse clinical outcomes but did not differ by metastatic status (53% of metastatic vs 60% of non-metastatic tumors). Within the corticotroph lineage, gene-level alterations in TP53, ATRX, and/or DAXX captured corticotrophs with recurrent chromosomal loss-of-heterozygosity (rcLOH), and were associated with shorter PFS (10.1 vs 149.9 months; p=0.009) and OS (116.6 months vs not reached [NR]; p=0.022). A subset of corticotrophs lacking rcLOH harbored gain-of-function USP8 mutations and were associated with longer PFS (149.9 vs 11.5 months; p=0.022). In lactotroph PitNETs, TP53, ATRX, and/or SF3B1 mutations were associated with shorter PFS (4.6 vs 21.5 months; p=0.049). Cell-cycle alterations were enriched in metastatic PitNETs and may contribute to metastatic dissemination. Next-generation sequencing segregates aggressive PitNETs into prognostic subgroups.

papers.title: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor masquerading as intra-ductal papillary mucinous neoplasm: a case report.
papers.abstract: Pancreatic cysts are being commonly diagnosed owing to the increased utilization of radiological modalities for the evaluation of abdominal complaints. Cysts can represent an underlying benign, pre-malignant or malignant diagnosis, and making an accurate diagnosis is often challenging. Here we report a case of a pancreatic cystic lesion, provisionally diagnosed as intra-ductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) based on pre-operative and intra-operative findings, which on final histopathology turned out to be a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.
papers.journal: Revista de gastroenterologia del Peru : organo oficial de la Sociedad de Gastroenterologia del Peru

papers.title: Next-generation chimeric antigen receptor platforms for skin cancer immunotherapy: Biological rationale, therapeutic opportunities, and precision selection strategies.
papers.abstract: Skin cancers comprise a biologically diverse group of malignancies with distinct molecular alterations, immune landscapes, and mechanisms of therapeutic resistance. Although immune checkpoint inhibitors have improved outcomes, particularly in melanoma and Merkel cell carcinoma, primary and acquired resistance remain common, underscoring the need for complementary immune-based strategies. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-engineered cellular therapies redirect immune cells toward selected tumor-associated antigens. Despite the clinical success of CAR-T cells in hematological malignancies, their application to solid skin cancers remains challenging because of antigen heterogeneity, immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments, limited infiltration, and inadequate persistence. CAR engineering has expanded beyond conventional T cells, but clinical maturity varies: CAR-T therapy is established in hematological malignancies, whereas CAR-natural killer (CAR-NK) cells and CAR-macrophages (CAR-M) have entered early clinical investigation in selected cancers. CAR-dendritic cells (CAR-DC), CAR-B cells, CAR-natural killer T (CAR-NKT) cells, and CAR-γδ T cells remain predominantly preclinical or conceptual for skin cancers. Their proposed functions include cytotoxicity, innate recognition, phagocytosis, and antigen presentation, but clinical efficacy in cutaneous malignancies has not been established. This narrative review synthesizes target biology, evidence maturity, therapeutic limitations, and emerging engineering strategies. We also propose a hypothesis-generating framework for studying CAR-platform selection according to tumor subtype, antigen characteristics, immune contexture, and mechanisms of immune escape.

papers.title: A phase I/II study using cabozantinib and lanreotide as treatments for advanced GEP-NETs for which molecular targeted therapy or chemotherapy have failed (SCALET): TCOG T2221 study.
papers.abstract: Somatostatin analogs (SSAs) and targeted therapies have shown efficacy for advanced gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (GEP-NETs) in the past decades. To explore the therapeutic efficacy of SSA and targeted therapy combination, we conducted a phase I/II study to evaluate the toxicity and efficacy of cabozantinib and lanreotide in patients with advanced grade 1/2 or 3 progressive GEP-NETs for which molecular targeted therapies or chemotherapy have failed (SCALET trial). Lanreotide (120 mg) was given on day 1 every 4 weeks. A 3 + 3 design was used in phase I to determine the maximum tolerated dose of cabozantinib (40 or 60 mg daily). The primary endpoint in phase II was progression-free survival (PFS). The secondary endpoints were overall response rate (ORR), overall survival, and toxicity of this regimen. A total of 42 patients were enrolled and treated. Among the 10 patients in phase I, no dose-limiting toxicity was observed. The recommended dose for cabozantinib was 60 mg daily for the 32 patients in phase II. Among the 31 patients evaluated per protocol, the median PFS (mPFS) was 25.2 months [95% confidence interval (CI) 6.7-43.7]. The mPFS in patients with pancreatic NET and extra-pancreatic NET were 27.5 months (95% CI 22.4-32.6) and 12.0 months (95% CI 7.2-16.8), respectively. The ORR was 35.5%. The median overall survival was not reached. These toxicities were comparable to those of cabozantinib and lanreotide reported in other trials. This phase I/II study highlights the efficacy of cabozantinib and lanreotide for advanced GEP-NETs (NCT05048901).

papers.title: Engineered T cell-agonist chimera for logic-gated STING activation and augmented cancer immunotherapy.
papers.abstract: The efficacy of adoptive T cell therapy against solid tumors is markedly hindered by the immunosuppressive microenvironment. Here, we demonstrate that stimulator of interferon genes (STING) activation in tumor-associated macrophages (TAM) enhances the intratumoral infiltration and cytotoxicity of adoptive T cells. We next design a TAM-targeted nanoagonist and engineer a T cell-agonist chimera (SNTC) via covalent surface anchoring, to achieve synchronized biodistribution of STING agonist with adoptive T cells. The nanoagonist is locally released in tumor tissue in response to the elevated reduction potential on T cell surface, followed by intracellular glutathione-mediated restoration of STING agonist in TAM, thereby enabling AND logic-gated STING activation. SNTC not only reshapes tumor stroma and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment to augment adoptive T cell function but also enhances the antigen presentation ability of TAM to activate endogenous T cells. SNTC elicits robust antitumor efficacy in melanoma tumor-bearing mice, resulting in over 40% survival beyond 60 d. Moreover, combining tumor-infiltrating T lymphocyte (TIL)-based SNTC with immune checkpoint blockade therapy leads to sustained tumor regression in mouse model of orthotopic pancreatic tumor. Collectively, SNTC holds translational potential to optimize STING activation for adoptive T cell therapy of cancer.
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

papers.title: Adjuvant PD-1 or PD-L1 blockade for Merkel cell carcinoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: To estimate the effect of adjuvant programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) or programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) blockade after definitive local therapy for Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) and assess certainty and applicability. We prospectively registered this systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD420261491127). Randomized trials comparing adjuvant PD-1 or PD-L1 blockade with no systemic adjuvant therapy after definitive local treatment for MCC were identified through six databases, registries, congress sources, reference lists, and citation searches through September 9, 2026. Two reviewers selected studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias and certainty. Hazard ratios (HRs) for recurrence or death were pooled using random-effects modified Hartung-Knapp inference. Four randomized trials were eligible; 3 trials with results included 572 participants. All point estimates favored blockade, but each confidence interval (CI) included the null. The pooled HR for recurrence or death was 0.70 (95% CI, 0.36-1.38). At a representative 24-month control event-free probability of 695 per 1000, this corresponded to 80 more participants per 1000 remaining event free (95% CI, 90 fewer to 184 more). Overall survival and safety could not be pooled. Certainty was very low for all critical outcomes. Adjuvant PD-1 or PD-L1 blockade may reduce recurrence or death after definitive local therapy for MCC, but evidence remains compatible with benefit, little or no effect, or harm. Routine class-wide use is not established; decisions should remain individualized pending mature survival and harmonized safety data. PROSPERO CRD420261491127.
